issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [X] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [X] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [X] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [X] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [X] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

> 简述：在 v26.10.17（与 main 相同）中，如果 XDRIVE 客户端在下载中途消失（进程被杀或断网），服务端无法察觉：它会继续从目标读取，并把剩余的整个响应写入存储（复现中 20 秒内写入约 235 MiB、607 个对象）。这些对象要等服务端的 mux 子连接自行结束后才会被清理（约 2.7–13 分钟），期间该会话仍被持续 LIST 轮询。原因是 XDRIVE 既没有对端存活检测，也没有背压。

Version: v26.10.17 (`92ccc93`, the newest release and the same commit as current `main`), `network: "xdrive"`, `service: "local"`. XDRIVE is only in the pre-releases since v26.9.30; it is not in v26.3.27. The session logic involved does not depend on the backend, so remote backends behave the same way.

When an XDRIVE client disappears in the middle of a download (process killed, network lost, which is common for mobile clients), the server does not notice:

1. It keeps reading from the target and writes the whole remaining response into the storage. In the repro the client had received 22 MiB of a 256 MiB body; within 20 s after the client was killed the server wrote 246,869,084 bytes in 607 objects.
2. These objects stay until the server-side mux sub-connection ends on its own: about 2.7 min when the target closes the connection after the body, about 13 min with a keep-alive target. Meanwhile the dead session is still polled (about 2 LIST per second).
3. The server logs nothing after the client is gone, even at `debug`.

With a remote backend every abandoned download can upload hundreds of MiB into the storage account, consume API quota and leave the objects there for minutes.

If only the application connection is closed while the client stays alive (curl killed), the server stops writing within about 5 s and the folder is cleaned up, so the problem is specific to the peer disappearing.

| 256 MiB body at 16 MiB/s, `sessionTtlSeconds: 30` | storage at +30 s | +90 s | +180 s | server kept writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| download completes (control) | 0 B | 0 B | 0 B | no |
| client `kill -9` after ~2 s | 246,869,084 B / 607 objects | same | same | yes, the whole remaining body |
| client `SIGTERM` after ~2 s | 246,394,446 B / 515 objects | same | same | yes |
| curl killed, client alive | 0 B (one `.end`) | 0 B | 0 B | no, stopped within ~5 s |
| client `kill -9`, keep-alive target, watched 900 s | 246,453,796 B | same | same | yes; empty only at ~750–780 s |
| client `kill -9`, target sends `Connection: close` | 246,485,923 B | same | 0 B | yes; empty at ~165 s |

**Cause**

- `Listener.claim` marks the session active (`transport/internet/xdrive/xdrive.go:225`); the mark is removed only in the connection's `onClose` (`xdrive.go:234`). `collect()` skips active sessions (`xdrive.go:267-269`), so the folder of a dead session is not collected while the server-side connection is open.
- That connection is closed only when the inbound handler returns (`app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go:123-127`), i.e. after the server-side mux session ends. XDRIVE has no peer liveness signal: no heartbeat, no idle timeout. `Conn.receive` blocks on the reader channel (`conn.go:53-61`), `walReader.poll` returns quietly on an empty listing (`wal.go:295-297`), `holeTimeout` fires only when later segments exist (`wal.go:312-321`), EOF comes only from a `.end` object (`wal.go:365`).
- No backpressure: `walWriter.Write` appends to the buffer and `flushLocked` starts `go w.upload` (`wal.go:73-91`, `wal.go:127-156`); the semaphore in `upload` limits concurrent `Put`s, not unconsumed data (`wal.go:161-166`). Segments are deleted only by the peer's reader, so nothing limits what

issues.title: XMC: 20 Hz tick-driven data shaping / XMC：20Hz 按 tick 驱动的数据整形
issues.body:
> **Revision note / 修订说明**
>
> This issue originally proposed splitting the XMC config into `clients`/`servers` blocks. After the discussion (RPRX: the split has no clear advantage yet, keep the config as-is; switch the data path to 20 Hz instead, breaking is fine), the split was dropped and the PR #7456 was repurposed. To avoid opening a duplicate issue, this issue is updated in place: the title and description now track the 20 Hz data shaping.
>
> 本 issue 最初提出把 XMC 配置拆成 `clients`/`servers` 区块。讨论后（RPRX：暂时没看到拆分的明显优势，配置先别动；改为 20Hz 发数据，可以 breaking），拆分方案已放弃，#7456 也随之改成了 20Hz 实现。为避免再开一个重复 issue，这里直接原地更新标题和说明，改为跟踪 20Hz 数据整形。

### Problem / 问题

After the login/configuration handshake, XMC currently wraps proxy writes in `xmc:data` custom payloads immediately (up to 24 KiB each). An idle connection therefore emits no packets, and a busy one becomes a bulk TCP stream.

Real Minecraft is not a bandwidth-driven stream; it is a 20 TPS (50 ms) clock:

- both directions keep sending small packets even while idle (the client's per-tick packet, the server's entity/world updates);
- [Tick#Game process](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Tick#Game_process) flushes queued packets once per tick;
- chunk loading is tick-shaped too: [Chunk Batch Received](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Chunk_Batch_Received) reports a "chunks per tick" rate, the server waits for batch acknowledgements, and [Chunk Batch Finished](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Chunk_Batch_Finished) targets roughly half of the available bandwidth;
- the 26.3 capture in #7423 shows packet rates near multiples of 20/s in both directions: idle c2s 21 pkt/s / 89 B/s, s2c 41 pkt/s / 5.6 KB/s; running 43/697 and 99/69K; join 2.2 MB / 12 s.

XMC 目前握手完成后会立即把代理写入封成 `xmc:data` 载荷（每块最多 24 KiB）：空闲时没有包，忙时就是一条 bulk TCP 流。

真实 Minecraft 不是带宽驱动的流，而是 20 TPS（50ms）的时钟：

- 空闲时双向也持续有小包（客户端每 tick 的包、服务端的实体/世界更新）；
- [Tick#Game process](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Tick#Game_process) 每 tick 才 flush 一次队列里的包；
- 区块加载同样按 tick 整形：[Chunk Batch Received](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Chunk_Batch_Received) 上报的是 "chunks per tick"，服务端要等 batch ack，[Chunk Batch Finished](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Chunk_Batch_Finished) 还把目标压在约一半带宽；
- #7423 的 26.3 抓包显示双向包率都接近 20/s 的整数倍：挂机 c2s 21 包/s / 89 B/s、s2c 41 包/s / 5.6 KB/s；跑动 43/697 与 99/69K；进服 2.2 MB / 12 s。

### Proposal / 方案（implemented in #7456）

After the handshake, queue proxy writes and flush them once per 50 ms game tick:

- every tick writes one small `xmc:pad` frame, so an idle connection keeps the 20 Hz cadence in both directions;
- queued data is split into `xmc:data` payloads of at most 24 KiB and emitted inside the same tick batch;
- no artificial bandwidth cap: a busy tick may carry several payloads, like a Minecraft chunk burst;
- `Close` flushes the queued tick before closing the connection, so the last bytes are not dropped.

The startup `paddings` schedule and the configuration format are unchanged. This is a breaking wire change for XMC (old and new peers do not pair), which is acceptable for a finalmask mask.

握手完成后把代理写入入队，每 50ms 游戏 tick flush 一次：

- 每个 tick 固定发一个小 `xmc:pad` 帧，保证空闲时双向都有 20Hz 节拍；
- 队列数据按 24 KiB 拆成 `xmc:data` 载荷，在同一个 tick 批次里发出；
- 不设人为带宽上限：忙的 tick 可以带多个载荷，像 MC 的区块 burst；
- `Close` 前先 flush 队列，避免最后几个字节丢失。

启动阶段的 `paddings` 预置和配置格式不变。对 XMC 是 breaking 的线格式变更（新旧端不能互配），对 finalmask 来说可以接受。

### Scope / 范围

- One padding frame per tick per direction for now; the packet-count/size distribution is not yet state-dependent (idle/walk/loading).
- The vanilla chunk-batch/credit shape is not reproduced yet; this change only adds the 20 Hz cadence.
- The config split (`clients`/`servers`) is dropped; see the revision note.

issues.title: Policy: Add `udpIdle` for the UDP dispatcher and inbound UDP sessions
issues.body:
## Problem

Two UDP idle timers are hard-coded. No policy setting changes them:

| Where | Today | What it ends |
|---|---|---|
| `transport/internet/udp/dispatcher.go` (`getInboundRay`) | `time.Minute` | a UDP flow relayed for the Shadowsocks, SOCKS and Trojan inbounds that gets **no response** for 60 s. Only downlink datagrams reset this timer. |
| `app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go` (`udpWorker.clean`) | `2*60` | a client's session on a UDP inbound listener (Shadowsocks, Shadowsocks 2022, Tunnel, ...) silent in both directions for 2 minutes |

TCP and most other UDP paths already follow the level's `connIdle` (freedom, VLESS, VMess, Trojan's outer timer, the native Shadowsocks 2022 sessions). These two timers ignore it, so raising `connIdle` has no effect on them.

### Why the constants hurt mobile and NAT users

Many UDP applications stay quiet for longer than a minute and expect the flow to survive: VoIP and messaging apps between calls, games between rounds, QUIC connections and VPN-in-proxy setups that send keepalives every 2–5 minutes, and P2P apps waiting for a peer. Mobile carriers' CGNATs commonly keep UDP mappings for several minutes, and so does Linux conntrack (`nf_conntrack_udp_timeout_stream`, 120–180 s by default and often raised).

When the dispatcher drops the flow after 60 s without a response, the next datagram the client sends opens a **new** outbound flow, which goes out from a new source port. The far end still sends to the old port, so its datagrams are lost. The application sees a dead path even though every NAT on the way still had a mapping for it. The 2-minute inbound limit has the same effect on the client side. Long-idle UDP over these inbounds can't currently be made to work, short of patching the binary.

Possibly related reports: #129 (Shadowsocks UDP: a game disconnects after each match) and #7386 (which describes the 2-minute cone-session cleanup in `worker.go`).

## Design

Add one policy field per level, `udpIdle` (seconds), next to `connIdle`:

```json
"policy": {
  "levels": {
    "0": { "connIdle": 300, "udpIdle": 60 }
  }
}
```

- **`features/policy`**: add `Timeout.UDPIdle`. `SessionDefault()` sets it to 60 s, which is today's value.
- **`app/policy`**: add proto field `udp_idle = 5` (regenerated with `infra/vprotogen`), plus the default, override and conversion code. `ToCorePolicy` only copies it when it is set, so a policy proto built without the field keeps the 60 s default instead of becoming 0.
- **`infra/conf`**: parse JSON `udpIdle`.
- **`transport/internet/udp.Dispatcher`**: add `SetIdleTimeout(d)`. The flow timer uses that value. Zero or negative, or never called, means 60 s. The package can't look up the policy manager itself because `core` imports it, so callers pass the value:
  - Shadowsocks: the user's level, set on the first authenticated packet. The user isn't known until then.
  - SOCKS: the inbound's `userLevel`, through the existing `s.policy()`.
  - Trojan: the session policy it already has.
  - The DNS UDP name server keeps the 60 s default (no change).
- **Inbound UDP listener (`udpWorker`)**: its idle limit is `2 × udpIdle` at level 0. That gives 120 s by default, the same as today's `2*60`, and keeps the client session outliving the flows it carries in the same ratio as now. Level 0 is used because the listener creates sessions before any proxy has authenticated a user.

Why a new field rather than reusing `connIdle`: `connIdle` defaults to 300 s. Applying it to these timers would change UDP behaviour for every existing deployment, from 60 s/120 s to 300 s/600 s, and would hold more UDP state on busy servers. A separate field keeps today's behaviour unless it is opted into. It also lets operators keep long TCP idle times (for example 1800 s) without keeping UDP that long.

## Compatibility

- Without `udpIdle`, every timer is exactly what it is today: 60 s for the dispatcher and 120 s for the inbound UDP session. A level that sets other fields but not `udpIdle` al

## Summary

`WriteAddressPort` runs on every UDP packet in XUDP, VLESS Multiplex and the
UDP paths of SOCKS, Shadowsocks and Shadowsocks 2022, and once per connection
in the VLESS, Trojan and VMess headers. It now writes the address and port
straight into the `*buf.Buffer` with **zero allocations** instead of three,
and is **3–7× faster**.

## Changes

- `AddressSerializer.WriteAddressPort` takes a `*buf.Buffer`, the same as
  `ReadAddressPort` already does. All 20 callers in the repository already pass
  one, so none of them change. `shadowsocks_2022.WriteAddressPort` follows.
- `writeAddress` and `writePort` write with `WriteByte`, `Write` and
  `WriteString`, so no temporary slices (`[]byte{tb}`, `[]byte(domain)`, the
  port array in `serial.WriteUint16`) escape to the heap any more.
- New `net.AppendIP(b, address)` appends the IP without the allocation that
  `address.IP()` makes for the `[4]byte` / `[16]byte` addresses of the package.

## Allocations

Checked with `testing.AllocsPerRun` in the tests, for IPv4, IPv6 and domain
addresses, port-first and port-last:

| Path | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `WriteAddressPort` into `*buf.Buffer` | 3 (8–20 B) | 0 |
| `net.AppendIP` | — | 0 |

benchstat medians, all p=0.002.

issues.title: TLS config: Fix race between certificate reload and handshakes
issues.body:
## Summary

Every TLS server with certificate files reloads them in the background: once an
hour by default, or at the `ocspStapling` interval, when it also refreshes the
OCSP staple. This PR makes that reload safe to run alongside live handshakes:

- **Handshakes always see a whole certificate.** The reload goroutine replaced
  the certificate in a slice that `GetCertificate` read without
  synchronization, starting right at listener start-up. Each certificate now
  sits in an `atomic.Pointer`, so a handshake gets either the previous
  certificate or the new one, never a half-written slot.
- **OCSP refresh no longer touches a certificate in use.** The new staple was
  written straight into the `*tls.Certificate` that handshakes were already
  sending, so a handshake could send a torn `OCSPStaple` slice header. The
  refresh now stores a copy with the new staple, and handshakes in flight
  finish with the certificate they started with.
- **`go test -race` is green again** for `Test_ListenXHAndDial_TLS`, which hit
  this race on `main`.

## Changes

- `buildCertificates` (unexported) returns one `atomic.Pointer[tls.Certificate]`
  per certificate. The reload goroutine stores into it, and
  `getNewGetCertificateFunc` loads from it.
- An OCSP update builds `newCert := *cert` with the new staple and stores it.
- `loadKeyPair(entry)` parses a key pair. It is the former `getX509KeyPair`
  closure, now shared by both builders.
- `BuildCertificates` keeps its signature and returns the certificates as
  loaded, without starting reload goroutines. `GetTLSConfig` is what keeps
  certificates fresh. Nothing in the repository calls `BuildCertificates`.
  Before, a caller's slice was updated in place by a goroutine it could not
  stop, racing with any read of that slice.

## Testing

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./transport/internet/tls`, `go run ./infra/vformat`
- `go test -race ./transport/internet/tls/...`
- `go test -race -run 'Test_ListenXHAndDial_TLS$' ./transport/internet/splithttp`
- `go test ./infra/conf/... ./transport/internet/...`
- New tests in `transport/internet/tls`:
  - `TestCertificateHotReload` swaps the certificate files on disk and
    reads the certificate through `GetCertificate` until the new one shows
    up. On `main` it passes without `-race`, so the reload works as before,
    and fails under `-race`.
  - `TestCertificateOCSPUpdate` serves a fresh OCSP response every second
    from a local server. It keeps the certificate returned before an update
    and checks that its staple did not change while the new staple arrived.
    It fails on `main` with `OCSP update changed the certificate in use: 1 -> 2`,
    with and without `-race`.
- I also ran the OCSP test against this branch with the in-place staple write
  put back. It fails with the same message, so the test pins the copy.

| Test | This PR | `main` | `main`, `-race` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `TestCertificateHotReload` | pass | pass | fail (race) |
| `TestCertificateOCSPUpdate` | pass | fail | fail |

issues.body:
## Summary

`buf.SplitSize` cuts the beginning of a `MultiBuffer` at a byte limit. It runs
on the hot path of several transports:

- **VLESS Multiplex**, sending: `encodeBatch` cuts every TCP frame of up to
  8 KiB from the pending data. This covers VLESS and VMess with Mux, VLESS
  Reverse and XDRIVE.
- **VLESS Multiplex**, receiving: `BufferedReader.ReadAtMost` reads every frame
  payload through it.
- **XHTTP** upload: the dialer cuts every POST of up to `maxUploadSize`, under
  any protocol carried over XHTTP.

Each call used to build a new slice for the taken buffers with `append` from
`nil`, which is one allocation per frame and several per XHTTP upload. Now
`SplitSize` returns both parts as slices of the input array: **zero
allocations** when whole buffers are taken, and **7–15× faster**. The code is
shorter too: the loop is 7 lines instead of 18.

## Changes

- `SplitSize` counts how many whole buffers fit into `size` and returns
  `mb[n:], mb[:n:n]`. The taken part is capped at `n`, so appending to either
  part can never overwrite the other, and the rest always starts after the
  taken buffers.
- When the first buffer is larger than `size`, it is still copied into a new
  buffer, as before.
- The doc comment states the contract: both results may share the array of
  `mb`, so `mb` must not be used after the call.

## API

The results of `SplitSize` are unchanged for every input. Two details of how
it treats the input array differ:

- The taken entries of the input array are no longer set to `nil`, because
  they are now the returned part. Code outside Xray that keeps the slice it
  passed in and releases it afterwards, for example with
  `defer buf.ReleaseMulti(mb)`, would release those buffers twice. Every
  caller in the repository reassigns the rest and never touches the input
  again.
- When everything fits, the rest is the empty `mb[n:]` instead of `mb[:0]`.
  Returning `mb[:0]` would let an append to the rest overwrite the taken
  buffers.

## Allocations

| Path | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Multiplex TCP frame of whole buffers (send; receive when the frame ends with a buffer) | 1 | 0 |
| 1 MiB XHTTP upload (128 buffers) | 5 | 0 |

## Benchmarks

Go 1.27.4, linux/amd64, Intel Core Ultra 7 266V, `-count=6`, benchstat
medians, all p=0.002. Buffers are `buf.Size` (8 KiB) each.

| Benchmark | Time | Allocs/op |

| 1 buffer, 8 KiB limit (Multiplex frame) | 42.2 → 6.2 ns (−85%) | 1 → 0 |
| 3 buffers, cut into 8 KiB pieces | 120.5 → 15.5 ns (−87%) | 3 → 0 |
| 128 buffers, 1 MiB limit (XHTTP upload) | 1807 → 123 ns (−93%) | 5 → 0 (2 KiB → 0 B) |

)

issues.title: TUN inbound, common/net: Reduce allocations on every UDP packet
issues.body:
## Summary

With the TUN inbound, every UDP packet of the device — QUIC/HTTP3, DNS, voice
and video calls, games — passes through `handleUDP` on the way out and
`writeUDP` on the way back, whatever the outbound is (Hysteria, VLESS, Trojan,
freedom, …). This removes **3 allocations from every incoming packet and 2 from
every outgoing one**, and makes these paths **12–26% faster**.

No API changes: only a new helper is added.

## Changes

- New `net.AsNetipAddr(address)` in `common/net` returns the IP as a
  `netip.Addr` without the allocation of `address.IP()` (the value-receiver
  `IP()` of `ipv4Address`/`ipv6Address` moves the array to the heap). Used in
  `writeUDP` for both addresses, and in the MASQUE server.
- `net.IPAddress` logs a copy of `ip` on its invalid-length path. Before,
  escape analysis reported `leaking param: ip`, so every caller's slice went to
  the heap — in TUN that is `p.src.AsSlice()` and `p.dst.AsSlice()` on every
  incoming packet. Now `ip does not escape`, which benefits every caller of
  `IPAddress` with a stack slice.
- `handleUDP` takes `b.UDP = new(src)` in the socket branch instead of
  `&src`, so `src` no longer moves to the heap on the common `HandlePacket`
  path.

## Allocations

| Path | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `writeUDP` (to the TUN) | 4 | 2 |
| `UDPDestination(IPAddress(addr.AsSlice()), port)`, ×2 per incoming packet | 2 | 1 |
| `src` in `handleUDP` | 1 | 0 |
| `net.AsNetipAddr` | — | 0 |

## Benchmarks

medians, all p=0.002.

| Benchmark | Time | Allocs/op | B/op |

issues.title: VLESS Multiplex, common/buf: Read and write frame length without allocations
issues.body:
## Summary

Every VLESS Multiplex frame carries a 2-byte length — each TCP chunk of up to
8 KiB and every UDP packet, including XUDP. This applies to VLESS and VMess
with Mux, VLESS Reverse and XDRIVE, over any transport. The length is now
written and read with **zero allocations**, and reading it is **6× faster**.
DNS over TCP gets the same read path for its message length.

## Changes

- **Write:** the frame length is written with
  `binary.BigEndian.PutUint16(frame.Extend(2), …)`, the same way
  `FrameMetadata.WriteTo` writes its fields just before it, instead of
  `serial.WriteUint16`, whose array escapes through `io.Writer`.
- **Read:** new `BufferedReader.ReadUint16` reads the two bytes at once, like
  `io.ReadFull`, so it behaves the same with any `Splitter`. With
  `SplitFirstBytes`, both bytes come from one packet and the rest of it is
  dropped, exactly as with `serial.ReadUint16`. When the cached buffer holds
  more than two bytes and no `Splitter` is set, it decodes them in place.
  Otherwise it reads into a field of the reader, because a local array escapes
  through the `Splitter` func value.
- VLESS Multiplex (`readBlock`, `copyFramePayload`) and DNS over TCP call the
  new method. `readBlock`, `readPacket` and `FrameMetadata.Unmarshal` take the
  `*buf.BufferedReader` they already receive from their only caller,
  `carrier.run`.
- `encodeBatch` reserves room in `frames` for a header and one payload buffer
  per frame up front. Before, the slice started at `nil`, so the header filled
  it and the payload made it grow; a batch of four UDP packets grew it four
  times.
- `common/serial` and `BufferedReader.ReadByte` are unchanged.

## API

`FrameMetadata.Unmarshal` now takes a `*buf.BufferedReader` instead of an
`io.Reader`. Go code outside Xray that passes another reader, such as an
`io.MultiReader`, has to wrap it to compile:
`&buf.BufferedReader{Reader: buf.NewReader(r)}`, as `frame_test.go` does now.
Xray itself already passes this type. Configuration and the wire format are
unchanged.

## Allocations

| Path | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Frame length write in `encodeBatch` | 1 | 0 |
| Frame length read (VLESS Multiplex, DNS over TCP) | 1 | 0 |
| `frames` growth in `encodeBatch`, one TCP frame | 1 | 0 |
| `frames` growth in `encodeBatch`, four UDP packets | 3 | 0 |

as a change against main, because the machine was not idle during this run.

issues.title: VLESS Encryption, finalmask, Hysteria: Pool array pointers to avoid allocations
issues.body:
## Summary

This continues #7491. `sync.Pool.Put([]byte)` boxes the slice into an
interface and allocates its 24-byte header on every call (staticcheck
SA6002). After #7491, `common/bytespool` pools array pointers that go into a
`sync.Pool` for free. This PR moves the remaining slice pools onto the same
technique:

- **VLESS Encryption:** every `CommonConn.Write`.
- **finalmask** (xicmp, xdns, udphop): every packet.
- **Hysteria masquerade proxy:** every response copy.

After this PR, the repository has **no `sync.Pool` of `[]byte` left**. The code
is shorter too: 72 lines added, 94 removed.

## Changes

- **finalmask** (xicmp, xdns, udphop): the three local pools of 4096-byte
  slices are gone. They now use `bytespool.Alloc` and `bytespool.Free`, which
  have an exact 4 KiB size class. `Free` takes the capacity, so the
  `p[:cap(p)]` re-slicing is gone too.
- **xdns server:** a fragment now goes into the same pooled buffer. Before, it
  took one buffer from the pool and returned it unused.
- **Hysteria masquerade proxy:** `httputil.ReverseProxy` gets its 32 KiB
  buffers, also an exact size class, from `bytespool`. The pool type is now an
  empty struct with two one-line methods, with no `sync.Pool` field,
  constructor or capacity check.
- **VLESS Encryption:** the record buffer pool holds `*[5 + 8192 + 16]byte`
  array pointers. It keeps its exact size, whereas `bytespool` would round
  8213 bytes up to 16 KiB. The pool is now unexported (`outBytesPool`). It was
  only used inside `CommonConn.Write`, and an exported pool whose element type
  silently changed would turn an old `.Get().([]byte)` into a runtime panic
  instead of a build error.

## Allocations

| Path | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `CommonConn.Write` (VLESS Encryption) | 1 (24 B) | 0 |
| finalmask packet buffer Get/Put | 1 (24 B) | 0 |
| Hysteria masquerade proxy buffer Get/Put | 1 (24 B) | 0 |

medians.

| `CommonConn.Write`, 8 KiB / 20 KiB | within noise (AES-GCM dominates) | 1 → 0 |
| 4 KiB pool Get/Put as in finalmask, 1 thread | 19 → 7 ns | 1 → 0 |
| 4 KiB pool Get/Put as in finalmask, 8 threads | ~8 → 1.3 ns | 1 → 0 |

issues.body:
## Summary

Every raw TCP connection reads through `buf.ReadVReader` and writes through
`buf.BufferToBytesWriter` on Linux. That covers direct traffic through
`freedom` for every protocol, and the raw TCP inbounds of VLESS, VMess,
Trojan, Shadowsocks and SOCKS. Both paths allocated small objects on every
call, only because of how a callback and a `net.Buffers` value were passed:

- **Read:** `readMulti` passed a closure to `rawConn.Read`. The closure and the
  byte count it captured were moved to the heap on every readv. Now there are
  **2 fewer allocations per read**.
- **Write:** `WriteMultiBuffer` converted its slices to a local `net.Buffers`
  and called `WriteTo` on it, which moved it to the heap. Writing several
  buffers now takes **zero allocations** and is **3.3× faster**.

- `NewReadVReader` binds `r.readFD` once into a field, and the byte count
  lives in a field that `readMulti` resets before each read. `readMulti` passes
  the bound function to `rawConn.Read`, so nothing is built per call.
- `BufferToBytesWriter` keeps its `net.Buffers` in a field next to the
  existing `cache`, and `WriteMultiBuffer` calls `WriteTo` on that field.
- Data, errors and byte counts are the same for every input, including
  `rawConn.Read` errors, retries on `EAGAIN`, EOF and a write error midway.
- `ReadVReader` is meant to be used by pointer from `NewReadVReader`, as
  everywhere in Xray. The doc comment now says so, because the bound function
  refers to the original reader, so a copy made by value would read into it.

## Allocations

| Path | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `ReadVReader.readMulti` (excluding the returned buffers) | 2 | 0 |
| `BufferToBytesWriter.WriteMultiBuffer`, several buffers | 1 | 0 |

## Benchmarks

Go 1.27.4, linux/amd64, Intel Core Ultra 7 266V, `-count=6`, benchstat
medians, all changes p=0.002.

| Benchmark | Time | Allocs/op | B/op |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `WriteMultiBuffer`, two 8 KiB buffers | 88.3 → 26.7 ns (−70%) | 1 → 0 | 24 → 0 |
| `readMulti`, two 8 KiB buffers from a pipe | within noise (syscall-bound) | 5 → 3 | 140 → 112 |

The remaining 3 allocations in `readMulti` are the returned `MultiBuffer` and
its two `Buffer` headers, which the caller takes over.

import (
	"io"
	"os"
	"testing"
)

	pr, pw, _ := os.Pipe()
	defer pr.Close()
	defer pw.Close()
	rawConn, _ := pr.SyscallConn()
	reader := NewReadVReader(pr, rawConn, nil)
	data := make([]byte, 2*Size)
	b.ReportAllocs()
	for b.Loop() {
		pw.Write(data)
		reader.alloc.current = 2
		mb, _ := reader.readMulti()
		ReleaseMulti(mb)
	}
}

// WriteMultiBuffer of two buffers, as for a raw TCP connection.
func BenchmarkBufferToBytesWriter(b *testing.B) {
	x, y := FromBytes(make([]byte, Size)), FromBytes(make([]byte, Size))
	mb := make(MultiBuffer, 2)
	writer := &BufferToBytesWriter{Writer: io.Discard}
	b.ReportAllocs()
	for b.Loop() {
		mb[0], mb[1] = x, y
		writer.WriteMultiBuffer(mb)
	}

```

</details>

- `go test ./common/... ./proxy/... ./transport/... ./app/... ./testing/scenarios`

  - `TestReadVReaderReadMultiAllocs` reads two full buffers from a pipe through

    without calling the read function and checks that `readMulti` still

> Depends on #7501: the first two commits belong to it, the last commit is this PR.

## Summary

`buf.ReadVReader` reads every raw TCP connection on Linux and other POSIX
systems. That covers direct traffic through `freedom` and the raw TCP inbounds
of VLESS, VMess, Trojan, Shadowsocks and SOCKS. This PR makes it handle a
connection reset correctly and lets servers with traffic stats use it too:

- **No more hung reads on a reset.** `readv` treated every errno as "not
  ready" and asked the runtime to wait again. When the peer reset the
  connection while the reader was waiting, the poller had already delivered
  that event, so nothing woke the reader again. The read hung until the idle
  timeout (300 s by default), holding the connection, its goroutines and file
  descriptors. Now the reset is returned at once as
  `readv: connection reset by peer`.
- **A reset is an error, not a clean end.** A reset that came before the read
  used to end it with `io.EOF`, so an aborted transfer looked complete. It is
  now reported the same way as by `conn.Read`, by the first single-buffer read
  and by the splice path.
- **readv with stats.** `NewReader` unwrapped `stat.CounterConnection` only
  inside the `syscall.Conn` check, which the wrapper never passes, so with
  inbound or outbound stats enabled every TCP connection fell back to
  `SingleReader`. Servers with stats now read the same way as servers without:
  up to **4× fewer read syscalls** on bulk transfers.

## Changes

- `multiReader.Read` returns `(int32, error)`. The POSIX reader waits only on
  `EAGAIN`, retries `EINTR` and returns any other errno, which `readMulti`
  wraps as `*os.SyscallError("readv", …)`, so `errors.Is(err,
  syscall.ECONNRESET)` works as with `conn.Read`. The error lives in a field
  next to the byte count from #7501, so the read path still allocates nothing.
- `NewReader` unwraps the stats wrapper once, before its checks, as
  `NewWriter` already does:
  - TCP with stats gets `ReadVReader` on the inner connection; it counts the
    bytes itself, as before.
  - Packet connections with stats (UDP, unix sockets) get `PacketReader`
    through the wrapper, the same reader they get without stats.
  - Connections that are not a `syscall.Conn` (TLS and other wrappers) are
    still read through the wrapper, so their bytes stay counted. This is what
    #730 fixed, and it is kept.
- Windows keeps its behaviour: a `WSARecv` error still waits and the

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable response headers
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `responseHeaders` map (`map<string, string>`) to the XHTTP inbound settings, giving the server control over the headers it writes on responses.

Currently the hub hardcodes a set of response headers: the CORS block for the browser dialer (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`), `X-Accel-Buffering`, `Cache-Control` and the SSE `Content-Type`. With `responseHeaders` an operator can add, override, or remove any of them, as well as set arbitrary extra response headers.

## Semantics

- A key that doesn't collide with a default header is added to every response.
- A key that matches a hardcoded header overrides it.
- An empty value removes that header from the response entirely (including the hardcoded ones).
- When `responseHeaders` is unset, the behavior is byte-identical to before.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "responseHeaders": {
    "Server": "nginx",
    "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "https://example.com",
    "X-Accel-Buffering": ""
  }
}
```

## Why

- The CORS headers only matter for the browser dialer; a plain server deployment currently emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response, which is undesirable behind a specific origin and gets flagged by security reviews.
- Reverse-proxy and CDN setups sometimes require specific response headers (`Server`, `Via`, custom headers) or different cache semantics.
- Operators running behind intermediaries may want the response header set to stay consistent with the profile of the service they front, instead of carrying markers that no other service on that endpoint emits.

## Notes

- Server-side only; the client ignores it. It round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 — the header matches all existing `.pb.go` files (`check-proto` passes; I verified the unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain first).

## Tests

- `Test_SetResponseHeader`: default / override / removal via empty value.
- `Test_WriteResponseHeader_ResponseHeaders`: CORS default, override, removal, custom header addition, origin echo.
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: XHTTP: Cancel HTTP requests when streams close
issues.body:
Closing an XHTTP stream before response headers arrive can leave its HTTP
request running. Repeated stream cancellations can therefore accumulate
unfinished requests.

Give each stream its own cancellable HTTP request context and cancel it
when the stream closes. Preserve independence from the original dial
context and keep the shared HTTP client reusable after normal cancellation.
Also close the stream-up upload reader together with its connection.

Local validation on the v26.10.29 base:

- With an HTTP/2 server withholding response headers, closing 1,000 streams
  leaves 0 pending requests after the fix, compared with 1,000 before.
- Targeted lifecycle tests passed with the race detector.
- HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 compatibility tests passed without the race detector.

Full race runs also reproduced a pre-existing TLS/OCSP race on both the
baseline and patched builds.

issues.title: transport/internet: non-force DNS empty response is logged at error level without the domain
issues.body:
### What version of Xray did you use?
26.11.9 (676eaf6). For comparison: 26.3.27 (d2758a0).

### Which operating system and architecture?
Linux amd64, official `Xray-linux-64.zip` builds.

### Minimal config
```json
{
  "log": {"loglevel": "debug", "access": "none"},
  "dns": {"queryStrategy": "UseIPv4", "servers": ["https://1.1.1.1/dns-query", "localhost"]},
  "inbounds": [{"listen":"127.0.0.1","port":19090,"protocol":"socks","settings":{"auth":"no","udp":false}}],
  "outbounds": [{"protocol":"freedom","settings":{"domainStrategy":"UseIP"}}]
}
```

### Steps to reproduce
```bash
curl -fsSL -o x.zip https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/releases/download/v26.11.9/Xray-linux-64.zip
unzip -q x.zip
./xray run -c cfg.json &
curl -sS --max-time 8 --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:19090 http://ipv6.google.com/
```
`ipv6.google.com` is AAAA-only; an A query returns CNAME + NOERROR/NODATA. Repeat with the 26.3.27 binary.

### What did you expect?
The A query returns NOERROR/NODATA. Because `UseIP` is a non-force strategy, `DialSystem` continues dialing with the domain and the system resolver may even connect on an IPv6-capable host. The expected behavior is an informational log line (as in 26.3.27), not an error per retry:
```
[Info] proxy/freedom: failed to get IP address for domain ipv6.google.com > features/dns: empty response
```

### What actually happened?
26.11.9 logs the failure at error level on every retry, and the domain is missing:
```
2026/11/25 03:02:37.280261 [Error] [840701999] transport/internet: failed to resolve ip > features/dns: empty response
2026/11/25 03:02:37.658563 [Error] [840701999] transport/internet: failed to resolve ip > features/dns: empty response
```
26.3.27, same config:
```
2026/11/25 03:02:41.314476 [Info] [3525449037] proxy/freedom: failed to get IP address for domain ipv6.google.com > features/dns: empty response
2026/11/25 03:02:41.723299 [Info] [3525449037] proxy/freedom: failed to get IP address for domain ipv6.google.com > features/dns: empty response
```

Real-world case: Facebook netseer measurement names like `<uuid>-netseer-ipaddr-assoc.xy.fbcdn.net` are AAAA-only by design. Each app session produces up to 5 error lines per connection (freedom retries); with `loglevel: error` this is the only visible output, and journal-based monitoring alerts on it.

### Suggested fix
1. Log at info/debug when `sockopt.DomainStrategy.ForceIP()` is false; keep error for force strategies.
2. Include the domain in the message, e.g. `failed to resolve ip for <domain>`, so operators can filter or route it.
3. Or do not log `ErrEmptyResponse` at error level for non-force strategies at all; return the error to the caller and let it decide.

### Notes
- 26.3.27 resolved the name inside `proxy/freedom` and logged at Info with the domain; 26.11.9 moved the lookup into `transport/internet.DialSystem`, so the domain is lost.
- Because the strategy is non-force, the dial continues after the log, so on an IPv6-capable host the connection may succeed. This is log noise, not necessarily a failed connection.
- Reproduced with both official binaries on the same config; 1.1.1.1 returns NOERROR/NODATA for the test name.

issues.title: SS2022 (AES) UDP inbound: a UDP session is created before the packet is authenticated, so any junk datagram costs ~1.5 KB of memory until the next cleanup
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

On a Shadowsocks 2022 inbound with an AES method (`2022-blake3-aes-128-gcm` / `2022-blake3-aes-256-gcm`), single-user and multi-user, every UDP datagram of at least 43 bytes (multi-user) or 30 bytes (single-user) creates a `ServerUDPSession` before anything about the packet has been authenticated. The datagram does not have to come from a client or carry a valid key: random bytes are enough.

`MultiUserInbound.processUDP` (`proxy/shadowsocks_2022/inbound_multi.go`) and `UDPCodec.DecodePacket` (`proxy/shadowsocks_2022/packet.go`, used by the single-user inbound) decrypt the 16-byte header with the block cipher, which always succeeds, take the session ID from it and call `udpSessions.GetOrCreate(sessionID)`, then `CheckPacketID`, which allocates the 1 KiB replay window. Only after that is the EIH looked up (multi-user) and the AEAD body opened. When the packet turns out to be junk, it is dropped, but the session stays in the map.

Such a session never gets a link, so its inactivity timer never runs. It is removed only by `UDPSessionManager.cleanup`, which runs only when `GetOrCreate` creates a new session at least 30 seconds after the previous cleanup, and only for sessions idle for more than the timeout (500 s on both inbounds). On a server that receives nothing more after the junk, the memory is not released at all.

Measured with the official `ghcr.io/xtls/xray-core:26.11.9` image (`Xray 26.11.9 Custom (go1.27.4 linux/arm64)`), the server config below, 100,000 random 48-byte datagrams from one source at 4,000/s over loopback, heap read from the `metrics` pprof endpoint with `?gc=1`:

| inbound | HeapAlloc before | after 100k datagrams | 60 s later, no traffic |
|---|---|---|---|
| multi-user (AES-256) | 1.6 MB | 148.3 MB | 147.9 MB |
| single-user (AES-256) | 1.5 MB | 149.1 MB | 148.6 MB |

That is about 1.47 KB per datagram. A heap profile on `main` (b56ffef) attributes ~75 % to `(*ServerUDPSession).CheckPacketID` (the replay window) and the rest to `(*UDPSessionManager).GetOrCreate` and the sync.Map. On `main` I also left the server idle for 560 s after 50,000 junk datagrams: the 74 MB were still allocated, and they were freed when the next datagram arrived and triggered cleanup. Nothing is logged at any log level.

Not affected: `2022-blake3-chacha20-poly1305` (the whole packet is opened before `GetOrCreate`), and the relay inbound (random data does not match a destination EIH).

The cost is memory, not a crash or an authentication bypass: the junk is never dispatched. issues.body:
## Summary

`sync.Pool.Put` boxes a `[]byte` into an interface, which allocates the slice
header (24 B) on every `bytespool.Free` and every `buf.Buffer.Release`
(staticcheck SA6002). This puts array pointers into the pools instead: a
pointer goes into a `sync.Pool` without an allocation, and converting the
slice back with `(*[N]byte)(b)` is free.

No API changes.

## Changes

- `bytespool.Alloc` and `Free` use pools of `*[2048]byte`, `*[8192]byte`,
  `*[32768]byte` and `*[131072]byte`, the same size classes as before.
- `common/buf` takes its 8K buffers from `bytespool.Alloc` and `Free` instead
  of its own `GetPool(Size)` pool, so they are shared with other
  `bytespool` users as before.
- `GetPool` (`xray:api:stable`) keeps its `[]byte` pools, since its callers
  type-assert `[]byte` from them. Nothing in this repository uses it any
  more.
- Pool sizes are defined once as constants for both sets of pools.

## Allocations

Checked with `testing.AllocsPerRun` on every branch: each `Alloc` size class,
`Free` with standard and odd capacities, `New`, `StackNew`, `NewWithSize` and
`NewExisted` with `Release`.

| Path | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `bytespool.Alloc` + `Free` | 1 | 0 |
| `buf.StackNew` + `Release` | 1 | 0 |
| `buf.New` / `NewWithSize` / `NewExisted` + `Release` (escaping) | 2 | 1 |

The one left is the `*Buffer` itself.

## Benchmarks

Go 1.27.4, linux/amd64, Intel Core Ultra 7 266V (8 threads), `-count=10`,
benchstat medians, all p=0.000.

| Benchmark | Allocs/op | Time |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `bytespool.Alloc` + `Free` (2K/8K/32K) | 1 → 0 | ~37 → ~6.7 ns |
| `BenchmarkNewBuffer` | 2 → 0 | 70 → 8.3 ns |
| `BenchmarkNewBufferStack` | 1 → 0 | 49 → 8.1 ns |
| `BenchmarkCopy` | 5 → 4 | 166 → 148 ns |

`BenchmarkNewBuffer`, `BenchmarkNewBufferStack` and `BenchmarkCopy` are the
existing ones in `common/buf`; `New` is inlined there, so the `*Buffer` stays
on the stack.

		b.Run(strconv.Itoa(int(size)), func(b *testing.B) {
			b.ReportAllocs()
			for b.Loop() {
				Free(Alloc(size))
			}
		})
	}
}
```

</details>

issues.body:
## Problem

Xray's Hysteria 2 UDP forwarding allocates on every packet:

- `ParseUDPMessage` wraps each datagram in `bytes.Buffer` and uses `binary.Read` for the fixed header.
- The destination address is converted to a new string for every packet, even when it is unchanged.
- `UDPWriter.WriteMultiBuffer` allocates a new `UDPMessage` and a new address string for every packet.

Upstream Hysteria v2.14.0 addressed this in `HyNetworks/hysteria@c2b181e`: it parses the fixed header directly, reuses the last address string when unchanged, and reuses buffers. The release notes report about 30% more packets per second for small-packet upload. Xray's Hysteria implementation still uses the v2.12.2-era code.

## Proposal

Port the upstream optimization to `proxy/hysteria`:

- add `ParseUDPMessageReuseAddr` (direct header parsing with `quicvarint.Parse`, address reuse);
- keep `ParseUDPMessage` as a wrapper;
- reuse the packet buffer, parsed message, and destination in `UDPReader`;
- cache the destination string and stack-allocate the message in `UDPWriter`, using `errors.AsType` for `DatagramTooLargeError`;
- add regression tests for fragmentation, address changes, cache hits, and write fragmentation.

The branch also updates `apernet/quic-go` to `v0.65.1-0.20261109005002-2895f039137a`, the version used by Hysteria v2.14.0. This requires adapting `transport/internet/masque/connectip` to `http3.HTTPStreamer.HTTPStream() (*http3.Stream, error)`. The two changes are independent and can be split into separate PRs if preferred.

VLESS Multiplex, Reverse Proxy: Refactor to move code into VLESS; Mux only uses `settings.multiplex` in VLESS/VMess outbound
issues.body:
This PR moves Multiplex to `proxy/vless/multiplex` and VLESS Reverse to `proxy/vless/reverse`. VLESS, VMess, and Reverse share the same Multiplex implementation. These paths pass decoded traffic through `DispatchLink` without intermediate `pipe` links.

### Protocol support

**Outbound Multiplex is available for VLESS and VMess.** Other outbound protocols use ordinary connections. VMess uses the shared implementation for inbound and outbound Mux. Ordinary VMess TCP and UDP keep the direct path from #5143. Reverse now uses the VLESS implementation, and the old standalone Reverse application has been removed.

### VLESS and VMess outbound configuration

Add `multiplex` under `outbounds[].settings`, alongside the protocol's other settings. This fragment enables the shared pool for up to eight active streams per connection.

```json
{
  "settings": {
    "multiplex": {
      "concurrency": 8,
      "xudpConcurrency": 0,
      "xudpProxyUDP443": "reject"
    }
  }
}
```

- A positive `concurrency` enables the shared pool. A positive `xudpConcurrency` enables a separate XUDP pool. If only `xudpConcurrency` is positive, TCP uses ordinary connections. With `xudpConcurrency` omitted or zero, UDP uses the shared pool when available.
- Omit `multiplex` or leave both counts at zero to use ordinary connections. An empty object `{}` also leaves Multiplex off. The old `enabled` property has no effect. Negative counts are rejected.
- `xudpProxyUDP443` applies when there is a pool for UDP/443. The default `reject` reports `XUDP rejected UDP/443 traffic`. `skip` uses the ordinary path, and `allow` uses the pool. UDP/443 uses the ordinary path when there is no applicable pool.
- XDrive requires a positive `concurrency` unless Reverse opens its own carrier. The shared XDrive pool uses a minimum concurrency of `128`.

### Legacy settings and API

Xray ignores the top-level `outbounds[].mux` key. During JSON loading it writes one warning to standard output per outbound containing that key, including when `settings.multiplex` is also present. The new settings determine whether Multiplex is enabled.

> The legacy "mux" setting is ignored. To enable Multiplex for VLESS or VMess outbounds, use "settings.multiplex". If Multiplex is disabled, Xray will use ordinary outbound connections.

API clients set `multiplex` in the VLESS or VMess outbound protocol configuration. The old `SenderConfig.multiplex_settings` field is ignored.

issues.body:
Refs #7455. The config split proposed there was dropped after the discussion; this PR now carries the login and data-shaping work that came out of it.

## What changed

### 1. The login is a version table, not literals

Every packet id the mask writes or matches is the registration order of `LoginProtocols` / `ConfigurationProtocols`, so it now lives in one table (`protocol_table.go`), one row per release:

| Release | Protocol | Login Finished session id |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1.21.1 / 1.21.2·1.21.3 | 767 / 768 | no |
| 1.21.4, 1.21.5, 1.21.6 | 769–771 | no |
| 1.21.7·1.21.8, 1.21.9·1.21.10 | 772, 773 | no |
| 1.21.11, 26.1 | 774, 775 | no |
| 26.2, 26.3 | 776, 777 | yes |

Rows were not copied from a capture:

- 767–775: minecraft-data's per-version `protocol.json` (`data/pc/<version>/`), which stores the same registration order as `{id: packet name}`;
- 776–777: the official 26.2 / 26.3 jars, `LoginProtocols` and `ConfigurationProtocols`.

26.3 is the reason the table exists. It inserts `ClientboundPostEffectsPacket` at `0x0a` in the configuration clientbound list, after the keep-alive and before `store_cookie`, and the list has grown by four packets since 1.21.1. Every id the mask uses happened to stay put — the table makes the next move a one-line change instead of a diff of five files, and `protocol_table_test.go` pins every id.

### 2. The login is the vanilla 26.3 exchange

Decompiled from the official 26.3 jars (`LoginProtocols`, `ServerLoginPacketListenerImpl`, `ClientHandshakePacketListenerImpl`):

- client: loops over login packets instead of expecting a fixed order; requires the encryption exchange and refuses a server that asks it not to authenticate, because an offline-mode login has nothing to reproduce and no session to verify; answers login plugin requests with a null payload and cookie requests with an absent cookie; reports Login Disconnect reasons;
- `Login Finished` carries the connection session id from 26.2 on — the server writes one per process like vanilla, the client reads and ignores it, and trailing bytes are ignored because Mojang has appended a field to this packet before;
- server: selects its row from the handshake and rejects an unknown version with the Login Disconnect a vanilla server sends (`outdated_client` below 754, `incompatible` above), validates the player name the 26.x way (≤ 16 printable ASCII — the old "letters, digits, underscore" rule is gone), rejects the TRANSFER intent like a server with `accepts-transfers=false`, and answers status with the JSON of the version it reports;
- configuration state: answers Keep Alive, Ping and Cookie Request, and stops on a Disconnect instead of draining it silently. Ping/Pong carry a plain 32-bit integer (not a varint, unlike the packet ids); the mod bench caught exactly that, see below.

`Set Compression` is negotiated in both directions: the client switches to the compressed framing when the peer sends it (verified against a real server at `65536` and at vanilla's default `256`), and the mask's own server does not send the packet, which is the same wire as a vanilla server with `network-compression-threshold=-1`; the padding preset was captured from such a login, so the framings line up.

### 3. 20 Hz tick-driven data shaping (unchanged from the earlier revision)

After the handshake, proxy writes are queued and flushed once per 50 ms game tick:

- every tick writes one small padding frame on `xmc:pad`, so an idle connection keeps the 20 Hz cadence in both directions;
- queued data is split into `xmc:data` payloads of at most 24 KiB and emitted in the same tick batch, so a busy connection looks like per-tick bursts instead of a bulk TCP stream;
- `Close` flushes the queued tick, so a graceful shutdown does not drop its last bytes.

### 4. Configurable payload channels

`dataChannel` / `paddingChannel` (empty keeps `xmc:data` / `xmc:pad`), validated as Minecraft resource locations: namespace and path follow vanilla's rules, at most 128 bytes,

issues.body:
On Linux, `net.FindProcess` finds the owner of a socket by a `readlink` of `/proc/<pid>/fd/*` of each process. Thus each lookup costs about one `readlink` for each fd open on the system. On a system with many open files, a lookup can take seconds, and routing falls behind. See https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7417#issuecomment-7161507880 and the measurements in https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7417#issuecomment-7185615730.

A `process` rule needs to know only whether the owner is one of its processes. This pull request uses that:

- `net.FindProcessMatching(network, srcIP, srcPort, destIP, destPort, accept)` is `FindProcess` with a filter. On Linux, it calls `accept` for each process in `/proc` with its PID, name and executable path, and reads the fds of the process only if `accept` returns true. That costs one `readlink` of `/proc/<pid>/exe` for each process, in place of one `readlink` for each fd. If no accepted process owns the socket, it returns `ErrProcessNotMatched`.
- `ProcessNameMatcher` passes its match to `FindProcessMatching`. A rule such as `"process": ["xray/", "self/"]` now reads only the fds of Xray itself.
- On the other platforms, the system gives the owner directly. `FindProcessMatching` calls `FindProcess` and then `accept`, so nothing changes there.
- `FindProcess` (also used by Lua `FindProcess`) is `FindProcessMatching` with a nil `accept`, and works as before.

The second commit fixes a separate case. A socket in `TIME_WAIT` has no process and has inode 0 in `/proc/net/*`. A new socket can have the same local address. Then the lookup took inode 0, read the fds of all processes and found nothing. Lines with inode 0 are now skipped. As before, Linux matches only the local address of the socket.

**Changes in behavior**

- If no accepted process owns the socket, `ProcessNameMatcher` returns false and logs nothing. Before, it logged "no process found for inode" when the owner was not found. This also covers an owner that Xray can't see, for example a process in another PID namespace, or a process of another user when Xray does not run as root.
- If more than one process holds the socket (for example after `fork`), the rule matches when any accepted process holds it. Before, only the first holder in `/proc` was checked.
- Each lookup now reads the `exe` link of every process. If the owner comes early in `/proc` and the system has few open fds, the old lookup could stop sooner. On a system with many open fds, the new lookup is much faster.

**Measurements**

`BenchmarkFindProcess` (in this pull request) finds the owner of a UDP socket while another process holds 50000 fds. `FindProcessMatching` accepts only the PID of the owner, as `self/` does. `FindProcessMatchingNone` accepts no process, so it reads only the `exe` link of each process. It ran on a Linux machine under load, so each `readlink` was slower than on an idle system.

As asked in https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7417#issuecomment-7185815928 and https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7417#issuecomment-7187292720, this PR makes `net.FindProcess` itself fast on Linux and Windows, without a hook. The problem is in https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7417#issuecomment-7161507880: with about 223k descriptors, each new connection took about 0.5 s on Linux.

In short, measured on the same VMs before and after:

- Linux: a new TCP connection takes 9.3 µs instead of 2.79 ms (200 sockets of the process), and a new connection of another process with 100 connections 96 µs instead of 5.54 ms (median). With about 2570 processes, as in the linked comment, the median lookup takes 1.19 ms instead of 158 ms.
- Windows: a new TCP connection takes 7.3 µs instead of 207 µs (200 sockets) and 6.3 µs instead of 1.99 ms (2000 sockets).
- `FindProcess` keeps its signature, so each `process` rule and the Lua `FindProcess` get this without a change in the router, whatever the rule names.
- One finder serves all lookups under a mutex. The slowest case is a full search of `/proc` under the lock, as each lookup of main is: the first lookup after the start, or a socket of another user when Xray runs without root.
- The `/proc/net` and table lookups of main stay as fallbacks. "Behavior changes" lists how the results differ from main.

Why the size: the descriptor cache is most of the Linux code, and the gain comes from it. With `sock_diag` and the fix of the inode 0 alone, a lookup still reads the descriptors of the processes until it finds the socket: at 40 processes with 2500 descriptors, the median stays at 122.5 ms (main: 115.8 ms), against 0.34 ms with the cache. If you prefer smaller steps, I can split this into a Linux PR and a Windows PR, or drop the nsi.dll part: the cached tables alone take 89.6 µs for a new connection (median, 200 sockets; main: 198.5 µs, with nsi.dll: 6.7 µs) for a new connection (200 sockets).

### Linux

**Socket.** Netlink `sock_diag` finds the socket of a connection by its two addresses. The request has no `NLM_F_DUMP`, so the kernel answers it with a hash lookup. For UDP, the kernel finds the socket that gets a datagram from the remote address. A program that connects to a local proxy has the address of the proxy as the remote address of its socket. The finder thus remembers the last 4 loopback remote addresses, and for a loopback source it tries them after the given remote address. If no exact request finds a socket, the finder asks for the sockets with the local port: a dump that the kernel filters by the port. Without `sock_diag` for a protocol, the finder reads `/proc/net` as main does.

`github.com/vishvananda/netlink` v1.3.1 is in `go.mod`, but its `SocketGet` sends a dump request, which the kernel answers with a walk over all sockets of the family, and its package-level functions open a new netlink socket for each call. The finder keeps one netlink socket.

**Process.** Linux gives a new descriptor the lowest free number, so a new socket of a known process often gets the number of a socket that the process closed or one of its lowest free numbers. For each process that it has read, the finder keeps up to 256 socket descriptors and the 4 lowest free numbers. The search stops at the first match, as in main, and goes in this order:

1. The socket cache: one `readlinkat` checks the remembered descriptor of the socket.
2. The processes of the last 16 lookups. For the 4 newest of them, their found and known socket descriptors and 2 free numbers. For the others, a few of these.

4. A few likely descriptors of each other known process.

@anonymously-hidden, could you take a look at a few ways to simplify the `.110` design? I’d start by publishing the first frame in just one place. Now that `.110` can fetch neighboring frames independently, I’m also curious how much parallel range reads within a single frame still contribute. [Changes in `.110`](https://github.com/anonymously-hidden/Xray-core/commit/bc05c514ac192930d0de0eb26169c64a6f273dec)

<details>
<summary>Options and what I’d test</summary>

**1. Publish frame 0 once.** If the first bytes fit in the session announcement, let the announcement be the publication of frame 0. Otherwise, publish it in the ring as usual. In `.110`, both writes can happen, so the receiver can ACK the announcement bytes while the slot write is still in flight. A single publication removes that race from #7415. If the initial slot write is skipped, create that file the next time the slot is used. [Announcement](https://github.com/anonymously-hidden/Xray-core/blob/bc05c514ac192930d0de0eb26169c64a6f273dec/transport/internet/xdrive/xdrive.go#L143-L163) · [Slot write and ACK](https://github.com/anonymously-hidden/Xray-core/blob/bc05c514ac192930d0de0eb26169c64a6f273dec/transport/internet/xdrive/slots.go#L128-L163) · [#7415](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7415)

**2. Try one streaming GET per frame.** Keep fetching different frames in parallel and use `Range` to resume an interrupted read. That would remove the need to split a single frame into ranges, queue them separately, and handle multiple range requests receiving full `200` responses. I’d test this with a large download and connections of unequal speed. Parallel ranges may make a real difference there. [Current range reads](https://github.com/anonymously-hidden/Xray-core/blob/bc05c514ac192930d0de0eb26169c64a6f273dec/transport/internet/xdrive/drive.go#L655-L702)

**3. Test `xdrivePrev` separately.** It helps when the head frame’s metadata read stalls by carrying its descriptor in the next slot. In `.110`, later frames can already finish independently and trigger a retry of the stalled GET. I’d compare the two paths with a metadata stall specifically. If a regular retry restores the stream in about the same time, we could remove `xdrivePrev` and the separate path that buffers the whole hinted frame. [Metadata lookup and recovery](https://github.com/anonymously-hidden/Xray-core/blob/bc05c514ac192930d0de0eb26169c64a6f273dec/transport/internet/xdrive/slots.go#L522-L595)

**4. Try two storage modes.** Put small frames entirely in `description` and large frames entirely in the media body. Currently, frames above 14 KiB and up to 1 MiB carry the first 14 KiB in `description` and the rest in the body. That middle mode lets the first bytes arrive before the media GET finishes. I’d keep it if it makes ordinary responses noticeably faster during a bulk transfer. [Frame representation](https://github.com/anonymously-hidden/Xray-core/blob/bc05c514ac192930d0de0eb26169c64a6f273dec/transport/internet/xdrive/slots.go#L128-L137)

For all four options, I’d keep frame growth based on receiver progress, a cap on unacknowledged data, and slot reuse gated on both completion of the previous write and the receiver’s ACK. I’d compare each option individually against `.110`. Its measurements show faster first bytes but slower response completion under load, so I’d track both timings alongside sustained bulk goodput and Drive request counts. [`.110` measurements](https://github.com/anonymously-hidden/Xray-core/blob/bc05c514ac192930d0de0eb26169c64a6f273dec/transport/internet/xdrive/README.md#L84-L102)

</details>

@RPRX Yes, they conflict, but only in `common/net/find_process_linux.go`: both PRs rewrite the socket lookup there, and both use `sock_diag` for it. The Windows part of #7417 does not touch that file.

To be clear about #7417: it keeps the signature of `FindProcess` and takes no config. The router does not change, and the cache lives inside the finder.

The difference is in the second half of a lookup. Once the socket is known, main and #7492 read `/proc/*/fd` until they find its inode. #7417 remembers where each process keeps its sockets and looks there first.

I ran main, #7492 and #7417 on one Ubuntu 26.04 VM (2 vCPU, kernel 7.0) as root. All three builds have the benchmark file of #7417, and the binaries take turns in each run: 10 runs of `BenchmarkFindProcess`, 6 of the others. Median lookup time, median of the runs:

| Case | main | #7492 | #7417 |
|---|---|---|---|
| New TCP connection, 200 sockets in the process | 5.46 ms | 2.32 ms | 7.5 µs |
| New TCP connection, 2000 sockets | 9.33 ms | 5.05 ms | 7.4 µs |
| New UDP socket, 2000 sockets | 8.11 ms | 4.54 ms | 11.8 µs |
| Existing connection, 2000 sockets | 10.5 ms | 5.05 ms | 5.9 µs |
| Another process with 100 connections replaces one of them | 5.79 ms | 2.59 ms | 0.10 ms |
| 40 processes with 2500 descriptors each | 118 ms | 107 ms | 0.33 ms |
| Same, 99th percentile | 273 ms | 260 ms | 310 ms |
| Same, with 2400 more processes on the VM | 137 ms | 109 ms | 1.18 ms |
| Same, 99th percentile | 296 ms | 264 ms | 312 ms |

So #7492 roughly halves the time of main. In the process rows, the 99th percentile of #7417 is its first lookup: it searches `/proc` the way main does on every lookup.

If it makes the review easier, I can move the Windows part into its own PR, since it does not overlap with #7492. For Linux, either way works for me: rebase #7417 on #7492 and put the cache on top of its `sock_diag` code, or keep mine (exact requests without `NLM_F_DUMP`, one netlink socket for all lookups). Most of the Linux gain comes from the descriptor cache.

I checked `a8411275`. The `SplitFirstBytes` case now works correctly: both bytes of the length come from the same packet. `serial.ReadUint16` also keeps its original signature.

One detail worth mentioning in the PR description is what the `FrameMetadata.Unmarshal` change means for Go callers. It used to accept any `io.Reader` and now requires a `*buf.BufferedReader`. The frame test is a concrete example: it previously passed an `io.MultiReader` directly. External code doing the same will need to update that call to compile against the new version. Xray itself already passes the required type. The configuration and wire format are unchanged.

There may be one more allocation to save in `encodeBatch`. For a frame with data, the first append puts the header buffer in `frames`. In the case I measured, that filled the slice to capacity, so appending the payload buffer made Go allocate a larger backing array.

My suggestion is to reserve two slots in `frames` when the frame has data. The header and one payload buffer then fit without growing the slice. This only reserves space for two buffer pointers. The wire format stays the same.

I tried this on `a8411275` with a subsequent TCP frame carrying 300 bytes in one payload buffer. On Windows/amd64, allocations went from **7 to 6 per operation** and memory from **296 to 288 B/op**. The median across three runs went from **153.7 to 140.7 ns/op**.

Could you compare three cases on Linux: the first TCP frame, a subsequent frame with one payload buffer, and a frame whose payload spans multiple buffers? In the last case the slice still has to grow, so it would be useful to see whether reserving two slots helps there too.

Thank you for the careful comparison — you are right about point 1, and that was a regression. Two `ReadByte` calls on a `SplitFirstBytes` reader take one byte from each packet. I've reworked the read side in a8411275:

- `common/serial` and `BufferedReader.ReadByte` are back as on main, so the shared helper keeps its behavior.
- New `BufferedReader.ReadUint16` reads the two bytes at once, like `io.ReadFull`. When the cached buffer holds more than two bytes and no `Splitter` is set, it decodes them in place, which is close to your variant. Otherwise it goes through `io.ReadFull` into a field of the reader, so it allocates nothing on either path.
- `TestBufferedReaderReadUint16` covers your case: packets `01 02 09`, `03 04 09`, then `05 06` with `SplitFirstBytes` give `0x0102`, `0x0304`, `0x0506`. It also covers a stream across buffer boundaries, a truncated length and release of emptied buffers. The same cases pass with `serial.ReadUint16` on main.

On the signatures: `FrameMetadata.Unmarshal`, `readBlock` and `readPacket` take `*buf.BufferedReader`. Their only caller, `carrier.run`, already holds one. With `io.Reader`, the method would need a type assertion with a fallback that still allocates. The narrower type lets the compiler guarantee the allocation-free path instead. `serial.ReadUint16(io.Reader)` keeps its signature.

Linux numbers (Go 1.27.4, Intel Core Ultra 7 266V, `-count=6`, benchstat medians):

| | main | #7496 | #7496 + #7494 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Frame length read | 14.3 ns, 1 alloc | 2.3 ns, 0 allocs | 2.4 ns, 0 allocs |
| First TCP frame | 224.7 ns, 11 allocs | 217.8 ns, 10 allocs | 186.5 ns, 7 allocs |
| Next TCP frames | 185.0 ns, 8 allocs | 178.3 ns, 7 allocs | 174.6 ns, 7 allocs |

My benchmark creates a `Session` on every iteration, so each count is one higher than yours. The deltas match: 10 → 9 → 6 for the first frame and 7 → 6 → 6 for the next ones. I've updated the description with the first-frame benchmark too.

comments.body:
I like this change. When I worked on the Multiplex migration in #7364, we were already writing frame metadata directly into the buffer, but we kept `serial.WriteUint16` for the payload length. Your change removes one more allocation per data frame. I’d keep the write side as it is.

I compared a few read-side variants and found one case worth covering before merging.

1. **Two `ReadByte` calls can produce a different value from one two-byte read.** With a `buf.BufferedReader` configured with `buf.SplitFirstBytes`, I supplied two packets containing `01 02` and `03 04`. The original code returned `0x0102` and left the second packet untouched. The PR returned `0x0103` and consumed both packets because the splitter releases the remainder of each packet after a read. The current Multiplex and DNS callers use the default splitter, but this changes the behavior of the shared `serial.ReadUint16` helper. I’d add a regression test for this case.

2. **Reading the pair together also benchmarks well.** I tried decoding both bytes directly when they’re already buffered, with a two-byte `io.ReadFull` at the buffer boundary. That preserved the packet behavior and let me keep the existing `ReadUint16(io.Reader)` and `FrameMetadata.Unmarshal(io.Reader)` signatures. On Windows/amd64, median time to read a buffered length was **15.63 ns/op** on the base commit, **5.70 ns/op** on this PR, and **4.68 ns/op** with the two-byte variant. Both optimized versions measured **0 allocs/op**. The variant does add a specialized buffer method, so I’d be interested in how that trade-off looks on your Linux benchmark.

3. **The first TCP frame is worth benchmarking separately.** In the posted `encodeBatch` benchmark, `s.first` stays `false`, so it measures a frame on an established stream. I also measured the first frame, which includes the destination address. Allocations per first frame were **10 on base, 9 with #7496, and 6 with #7496 + #7494**. For subsequent TCP frames, the counts were **7, 6, and 6**. That makes the contribution of each PR clear.

My suggestion is to keep the direct write, cover the packet-boundary case, and try the two-byte read on your setup before narrowing the exported interfaces.

comments.body:
@RPRX, I ran 16 XDrive configuration cases on both [`67756b3`](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/67756b3674d56b72c7a7e675e8dcd3f883e1b2f7) and [`b56ffef`](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/b56ffef338c8096c7dbe78eaa76f1cb05a328d6f), the parent of the auto-Mux change.

`"skip"` does fail with `"concurrency": 128`. The case that passes is `"multiplex": {"xudpProxyUDP443": "skip"}` by itself. With both concurrency values at zero, normalization drops the entire `multiplex` block. XDrive then creates a new block with `concurrency: 128`, so the `skip` check sees an empty policy. `"allow"` is lost the same way, and UDP/443 falls back to `reject`.

<details>
<summary>Where the setting is lost in the code</summary>

1. `OutboundDetourConfig.Build()` builds the protocol settings before calling `validateXDrive()`. [Call order in `infra/conf/xray.go`](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/67756b3674d56b72c7a7e675e8dcd3f883e1b2f7/infra/conf/xray.go#L364-L383)
2. `MultiplexConfig.Build()` passes `xudpProxyUDP443` to `NormalizeConfig()`. If `concurrency` and `xudpConcurrency` are both zero, normalization returns `nil` even when the policy was explicitly set. [Builder](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/67756b3674d56b72c7a7e675e8dcd3f883e1b2f7/infra/conf/vless.go#L246-L256) · [Normalization](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/67756b3674d56b72c7a7e675e8dcd3f883e1b2f7/proxy/vless/multiplex/client.go#L20-L33)
3. `validateXDrive()` replaces `nil` with `vless.Multiplex{Concurrency: 128}` before checking for `skip`. `Client.Dispatch()` treats the resulting empty policy as `reject`. [XDrive default and validation](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/67756b3674d56b72c7a7e675e8dcd3f883e1b2f7/infra/conf/xray.go#L267-L274) · [UDP/443 dispatch](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/67756b3674d56b72c7a7e675e8dcd3f883e1b2f7/proxy/vless/multiplex/client.go#L75-L83)

</details>

<details>
<summary>Test results for all 16 configurations</summary>

I used the existing `TestXDriveOutboundConfig` fixture. For every accepted config I also called `Client.Dispatch` with a UDP/443 destination and a test callback to detect whether it tried to open a Mux connection.

On `67756b3`:

- No `multiplex` block, an empty block, or `reject` alone: config accepted, `128` applied, UDP/443 rejected.
- `allow` alone, `allow` with `concurrency: 0`, or `allow` with both concurrency values explicitly zero: config accepted, the policy becomes empty, UDP/443 rejected.
- `skip` alone or `skip` with `concurrency: 0`: config accepted, the policy becomes empty, UDP/443 rejected at dispatch.
- `allow` with `concurrency: 8` or `128`: policy preserved, UDP/443 reaches the pool's open callback.
- `skip` with `concurrency: 128`: config rejected. `reject` with `concurrency: 128`: config accepted, UDP/443 rejected at dispatch.
- With only `xudpConcurrency: 8` set as a concurrency value: `allow` is preserved and reaches the open callback, `skip` is rejected at config build, and `reject` is preserved and rejects UDP/443 at dispatch.
- An unknown policy is rejected at config build, even with both concurrency values at zero.

On `b56ffef`, configs without a positive `concurrency` were rejected, including the cases with a positive `xudpConcurrency` alone. The controls with positive `concurrency` behaved the same on both versions. [Auto-Mux change](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/c5ccb356aa5ef45335f633132e7cead664b8fce2)

</details>

comments.issue_title: Observatory: a stalled TLS handshake leaks goroutines on both sides of the probe
comments.body:
Still reproducible on current `main` (`b56ffef`), and both candidate PRs (#6582, #6583) are closed unmerged, so nothing has changed since the original report. `newHTTPClient` in `app/observatory/burst/ping.go` still builds the probe `http.Transport` from `h.ctx` with no `TLSHandshakeTimeout`.

Minimal repro, no second node needed: one `freedom` outbound, a `burstObservatory` probing it, and a probe destination that accepts TCP and never answers the TLS ClientHello (a listener that `Accept`s and reads into `io.Discard`). `pingConfig: {interval 2s, sampling 1, timeout 3s}`. Each probe times out at 3s, but the goroutine parked in `net/http.(*persistConn).addTLS` stays. Goroutine totals and the `addTLS` count from the `metrics` pprof endpoint, no other traffic:

```
 t(s)   goroutines   addTLS   HeapAlloc(KB)
    0           18        3           1643
   30           31       12           1747
   60           46       21           1853
   90           61       30           1936
  120           75       39           2019
  180           91       48           2126
  240          105       57           2218
```

One leaked `addTLS` goroutine per probe that hits a stalled TLS peer, none ever released; linear in time. On a node that keeps probing an outbound whose path is a censor that blackholes after the ClientHello (e.g. a CDN-fronted outbound that goes silent mid-handshake), this is a steady goroutine/connection leak with `probeInterval`-paced growth, which matters most on memory-constrained relays. A per-probe `TLSHandshakeTimeout` (as the non-burst observer already sets) plus propagating the probe timeout into the dispatched outbound's dial would bound it.

comments.issue_title: SS2022 proxy: Refinements & fixes
comments.body:
Thanks for picking this up — the session-before-auth and the source-change / concurrent-decode fixes all look good here.

One case from #7194 isn't covered yet: an oversized **downlink** datagram still ends the whole UDP flow instead of being dropped. In `UDPWriter.WriteMultiBuffer`, `EncodePacket` returns `ErrPacketTooLarge` once the SS2022-wrapped packet exceeds `buf.Size` (8192), and the writer does `return err`, so every datagram queued after the big one is discarded and the session's downlink stops until the client reconnects. It triggers on a normal upstream reply that is large after wrapping (a big DNS answer, some game traffic), not only on crafted input.

Minimal test (fails on this branch, the second datagram is never written):

```go
func TestUDPWriterDropsOversizedPacket(t *testing.T) {
	method, err := GetCipherMethod(MethodAES256GCM)
	common.Must(err)
	key := make([]byte, method.KeySaltLength)
	rand.Read(key)
	clientCodec, err := NewUDPPacketCodec(method, [][]byte{key})
	common.Must(err)
	serverCodec, err := NewUDPServerCodec(method, key, nil, time.Minute)
	common.Must(err)
	session, err := clientCodec.NewClientSession()
	common.Must(err)

	var out recorder // an io.Writer that appends each Write to a slice
	writer := &UDPWriter{Writer: &out, Destination: net.UDPDestination(net.LocalHostIP, 443), Session: session}

	large := buf.New(); large.Extend(buf.Size) // too big to fit one SS2022 packet
	small := buf.New(); small.Write([]byte("small"))

	if err := writer.WriteMultiBuffer(buf.MultiBuffer{large, small}); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("oversized datagram should be dropped, not end the flow: %v", err)
	}
	if len(out.packets) != 1 {
		t.Fatalf("expected the small datagram to still go out, got %d packets", len(out.packets))
	}
	_, decoded, err := serverCodec.DecodePacket(out.packets[0])
	common.Must(err)
	if string(decoded.Payload) != "small" {
		t.Fatalf("unexpected payload %q", decoded.Payload)
	}
}
```

A lower layer would drop a datagram that doesn't fit, not tear down the connection — so dropping that one packet and continuing (`if err == ErrPacketTooLarge { continue }`) keeps the rest of the flow alive. Happy to send it as a small follow-up if you'd prefer not to fold it in here.

I agree. I tried to solve a similar problem in my fork. I wanted to see directly from Go which node each flow was routed through, whether it was actually carrying traffic, and close selected flows on a particular node when needed.

Closing a flow was the easy part. The harder part was tracing where the flow lives and which component owns its resources. For example, a single UDP session can send packets through different nodes. Traffic needs to be accounted for per node, and closing the session should leave unrelated sessions alone. In the end, tracking and controlling flows added more than three thousand lines of code, excluding tests.

I looked at how a few other proxy cores handle this. Their main connection-tracking and control code is a few hundred lines, and it is easy to follow the path to the component that closes the connection. So I agree that Xray should start by passing the context from the transport to the handler and making it clear who owns the connection from open to close.
